content: In children under five years of age who have been in contact with individuals with active tuberculosis (TB), as well as in people living with HIV (PLHIV), testing for TB infection is not mandatory before initiating treatment. However, it is essential to rule out active TB disease before starting TB preventive treatment (TPT). Chest radiography can be a valuable tool in excluding active TB disease and increasing confidence in initiating TPT. Counseling is also a critical component of patient-centered care, enabling individuals to make informed decisions about TPT by understanding the potential benefits and risks of treatment. The 2020 update of the World Health Organization (WHO) TPT guidelines recommends multiple treatment options tailored to specific populations, such as children and PLHIV, in both highand low-TB burden settings. While additional tests (e.g., liver function tests) and supportive medications (e.g., pyridoxine) should be available if needed, they are not routinely required and should not hinder the scale-up of TPT. Until newer TPT regimens are widely available, countries should continue using older approaches, such as six months of isoniazid, for adults and children who require treatment. Individuals on TPT should receive active support to complete their treatment and maximize its benefits. Programs may organize in-person follow-ups and use communication technologies to support medication adherence, similar to strategies used for treating active TB. A person-centered approach should be prioritized, ensuring privacy and protection from stigma. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of TPT programs should focus on three key indicators: the coverage of contact investigations, the initiation of TPT, and the completion of TPT. M&E activities should be integrated into existing national health information systems, with an emphasis on electronic data capture to generate strategic information and collect patient-level data, such as adverse events and corrective actions. The Ministry of Health should establish or strengthen a national coordinating body or technical expert working group to support the scale-up of TPT services in alignment with global guidelines. This body should guide national efforts to fulfill commitments made during the 2018 UN High-Level Meeting on TB. It should include representatives from relevant government programs, civil society, technical partners, and individuals affected by TB. Regular meetings should be held to address ongoing priorities, with the national TB and HIV programs serving as the secretariat. When budgeting for TPT programs, key cost determinants include the estimated burden of TB, the investigation of target populations, human resources, medication costs, and adherence support. Advocacy, community engagement, and training for healthcare workers are also essential components of program implementation. Electronic tools should be developed or updated to capture key data elements for programmatic indicators and clinical management. The tuberculin skin test (TST) remains a widely used method for detecting TB infection due to its low cost and feasibility in resource-limited settings. Proper administration involves intradermal injection of tuberculin on the inner forearm, creating a wheal of 6–10 mm. The test should be read within 48–72 hours, measuring the induration (not redness) at the injection site. Interpretation of TST results depends on the individual’s risk factors and the size of the induration. For example, an induration of 5 mm or more is considered positive in high-risk groups, such as HIV-infected individuals or recent TB contacts, while 10 mm or more is positive in moderate-risk groups, and 15 mm or more is positive in individuals with no known risk factors. False-positive TST results may occur due to prior BCG vaccination, infection with non-tuberculous mycobacteria, or errors in test administration. False-negative results can occur in individuals with weakened immune systems, recent TB infection, or overwhelming TB disease. Two-step testing may be conducted to identify a boosted reaction in individuals with prior sensitization to mycobacteria, ensuring accurate interpretation of results for future comparisons. Adverse reactions to TST are rare but may include fever, injection site pain, or, in highly sensitive individuals, vesicles, ulcers, or necrosis. TST is contraindicated only in individuals with a history of severe reactions to the test. It is safe for use in infants, children, pregnant women, and individuals with HIV. Repeated TSTs are generally safe and may be necessary if the individual does not return for the initial test reading.
